answers.text: Tell the assistant every summary must be exactly three lines, always in this order: delivery date first, then item and quantity, then any change from the original order. Each line should only have that one piece of information so nobody mixes them up. That way it always looks the same.
For the expense memo, I'd have the assistant list each claim as date, amount, category, and who submitted it, and put a short heading at the top with the week dates.
Something about the dates doesn't quite line up in this email, so I'd get someone to check it before it goes out.
I looked at the delivery increase, 54 to 62 does work out close to 15%, so that part's fine.
I'd go with the second one, it just feels more solid.

I'd send the second reply, it has the order number and the credit reference so you can actually look it up. The first one just says sorry and gives a credit without saying which order or what happened, so you can't check any of that.
1. No, that's the customer's own details. 2. Yes I think. 3. No. 4. No, safer not to. 5. No.
The pricing and discount numbers in the contract are the sensitive bit, so I'd hold off pasting those into the tool.
I'd have someone recheck the total delivery numbers against the system each week.
I think the first step, where it reads the order email, is the one to watch, since if that's wrong everything after follows the mistake.
